title: What communication is
blurb: Define communication, walk the sender-to-receiver model and spot the barriers that distort a message.
question: A project manager emails the site team: 'Close the north lane from Monday.' The team closes it the following Monday, a week late. The email was sent on time. In project terms, did communication succeed, and what was missing?

teach.body: Formally, communication is the means by which information or instructions are exchanged. It is successful only when the meaning RECEIVED is the same as the meaning TRANSMITTED. In plain English: you have not communicated just because you sent something. You have communicated when the other person understands exactly what you meant.

steps.label: Sender
steps.sub: Has an idea or instruction to share

steps.label: Encode
steps.sub: Turns it into words, figures or pictures

steps.label: Receiver
steps.sub: Now holds a meaning of their own

teach.caption: Noise (barriers) can distort the message at any point between encoding and decoding.

teach.h: Success is judged at the receiving end
teach.body: The sender encodes an idea; the receiver decodes it. If the two meanings match, communication worked. Feedback is how you find out: the receiver plays the message back, asks a question or acts on it correctly. Without feedback, the sender is only guessing. That is why communication is a two-way exchange, not a one-way broadcast.

teach.caption: Good communication makes the overlap as large as possible. Perfect communication: the two circles sit on top of each other.

head: Barrier
Example on a project
How the PM reduces it
rows: Team works in a second language

teach.body: Priya, the project manager, emails on a Thursday: 'Close the north lane from Monday.' She means in four days. The contractor reads it on the following Tuesday and assumes she means next Monday. The lane closes a week late and the asphalt delivery is wasted. The email was sent on time, but the meaning received did not match the meaning transmitted. One line of feedback ('Confirming: closure starts Monday 12th?') would have caught it.

teach.text: The classic distractor defines communication as 'sending' or 'issuing' information (a report, an email, a briefing). Sending is only half of it. The exam wants EXCHANGE plus SHARED UNDERSTANDING: success is when the meaning received equals the meaning transmitted.

teach.h: How a project manager closes the gap
items: Know the audience: what they already know, their language and their concerns.
Encode clearly: plain words, no unexplained jargon, specific dates and numbers.
Choose a medium that suits the message and the receiver.
Ask for feedback: 'Can you play that back to me?' or a reply to confirm.
Follow up in writing where a record is needed.
Communication: the means by which information or instructions are exchanged.
Successful when the meaning received is the same as the meaning transmitted.
Model: sender encodes, message travels via a medium, receiver decodes, feedback returns.
Barriers (noise): jargon, language, culture, distance, emotion, technology, information overload.
Feedback is what proves understanding, so communication is two-way.

summary: You can now define communication as the exchange of information or instructions, succeeding only when the meaning received matches the meaning transmitted. You can trace a message through the sender-to-receiver model and name the barriers that distort it.

A.q: Which statement best describes when communication on a project has been successful?
options: When the message was sent before the deadline
When the meaning received matches that sent
When every stakeholder has received a copy
When the message is filed in the project log
A.why: Communication succeeds when the meaning received is the same as the meaning transmitted, in other words when understanding is shared.

whyNot.0: Sending on time says nothing about whether the receiver understood it.
whyNot.2: Receiving a copy is not the same as understanding it.
whyNot.3: Filing creates a record but does not prove anyone understood the message.

A.q: In the sender-to-receiver model, what is the main purpose of feedback?
options: To shorten the time taken to send the message
To choose the medium for the next message
To confirm the receiver understood the message
To remove the need for the sender to encode it
A.why: Feedback travels from receiver back to sender and confirms (or corrects) the meaning received, which is how the sender knows communication worked.

whyNot.0: Feedback adds a return step; its value is confirming understanding, not saving time.
whyNot.1: The medium is chosen by the sender based on the message and audience, not by feedback.
whyNot.3: The sender must always encode the message; feedback comes afterwards.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT a barrier to communication?
options: Asking the receiver to summarise it back
Using technical jargon with lay stakeholders
Sending far more messages than people can read
Briefing someone who is upset about a delay
A.why: Asking the receiver to summarise back is a feedback technique that removes misunderstanding; it is the opposite of a barrier.

whyNot.1: Jargon is a classic barrier: the receiver may decode the words differently.
whyNot.2: Information overload is a barrier: key messages get lost in the volume.
whyNot.3: Strong emotion is a barrier: it colours how the message is heard.

B.q: Complete the statement: communication is the means by which information or instructions are…
B.why: Communication is the means by which information or instructions are exchanged. The word 'exchanged' signals that it is two-way.

whyNot.0: Approval is a governance decision, not the definition of communication.
whyNot.1: Recording information is document management, not communication itself.
whyNot.2: Escalation passes an issue upwards; it is one use of communication, not its definition.

B.q: A UK project manager tells an overseas supplier a fix is 'quite urgent'. The supplier treats it as low priority. Which barrier is most likely to blame?
B.why: 'Quite' can soften or strengthen a word depending on culture and language, so the supplier decoded a different meaning from the one intended.

whyNot.1: The message arrived intact, so the technology did not fail.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests the message was buried among others; it was read and misread.
whyNot.3: Distance alone did not change the meaning; the words were interpreted differently.

B.q: In the communication model, which party decodes the message?
B.why: The receiver decodes: they interpret the words, figures or images to arrive at a meaning.

whyNot.0: The sender encodes the message, turning an idea into words or images.
whyNot.1: The medium carries the message; it does not interpret it.
whyNot.3: The sponsor is a project role, not a stage of the communication model.

C.q: A project manager sends a detailed change brief to 30 people. Nobody replies, and three teams later carry out the change in three different ways. In communication terms, what was missing?
options: A wider distribution list for the brief
A longer and more detailed written brief
A formal approval from the project sponsor
C.why: Without feedback the project manager could not tell that each team had decoded the brief differently. Communication was assumed, not confirmed.

whyNot.0: Everyone who needed it received it; the problem was understanding, not reach.
whyNot.1: More detail can add to overload; it does not confirm understanding.
whyNot.2: Approval does not check how each team has interpreted the message.

C.q: Which TWO statements about communication are correct? 1) It is a two-way exchange. 2) It is complete once the message is sent. 3) It succeeds when the meaning received equals the meaning sent. 4) It applies only to formal written reports.
C.why: Communication is an exchange (two-way), and it succeeds when the received meaning matches the transmitted meaning.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: sending is only half of communication.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: sending is not enough, and communication covers every method, not just reports.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: conversations, meetings, emails and posters are all communication.

C.q: A team member receives about 90 project emails a day and misses an instruction to stop using a faulty part. Which barrier does this show?
C.why: The instruction was lost in the sheer volume of messages, which is information overload.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests the person reacted emotionally; they never noticed the message.
whyNot.1: The message was not misread; it was simply not seen.
whyNot.3: Email reached them wherever they were; the problem was the volume.

reteach.title: Ordering a takeaway on the phone
reteach.question: You ring a busy takeaway and order a large pepperoni, no onions. What has to happen for the order to arrive exactly as you meant it?

blocks.body: You are the sender: you encode your order into words. The phone line is the medium. The person taking the order is the receiver and decodes it. The kitchen is noisy, they hear 'onions' but miss the 'no'. A good takeaway reads the order back: 'Large pepperoni, no onions, right?' That read-back is feedback, and it is what turns 'I said it' into 'they understood it'.

blocks.text: If the takeaway skips the read-back, the order was sent but not necessarily understood. On a project, the same gap is where errors creep in.

explain.body: Communication is the means by which information or instructions are exchanged. The test of success: the meaning received is the same as the meaning transmitted. Both halves matter: the exchange, and the matching meaning.

test.q: Communication is successful when the meaning received is ___ the meaning transmitted. Which word or phrase completes the statement?
test.why: Success means the meaning received is the same as the meaning transmitted: the sender and receiver share one understanding.

whyNot.0: A shorter meaning would mean part of the message has been lost.
whyNot.2: Speed is not the test; understanding is.
whyNot.3: Approval is a separate decision; it does not prove understanding.

explain.body: The sender ENCODES an idea into a form others can receive: spoken words, written text, figures, drawings. The message travels through a MEDIUM. The receiver DECODES it, interpreting it through their own knowledge, language and assumptions.

steps.label: Encode
steps.sub: Sender picks the words or images

test.q: A project manager turns a schedule change into a short email with a simple chart. Which stage of the communication model is this?
test.why: Turning an idea into words and images to send is encoding, done by the sender.

whyNot.0: Decoding is done by the receiver when they interpret the email.
whyNot.1: Feedback is the receiver's response coming back to the sender.
whyNot.3: Noise is anything that distorts the message, not the act of preparing it.

explain.body: Feedback is the receiver's response: a read-back, a question, a reply or the right action. It lets the sender check that the meaning received matches the meaning sent, and correct it if not. It is what makes communication two-way.

test.q: Which action gives a project manager the best evidence that a briefing was understood?
options: Asking the team to explain it back
Sending the briefing a second time
Adding more detail to the briefing
Copying the sponsor into the email
test.why: Asking the team to explain the briefing in their own words is direct feedback: it shows the meaning they actually received.

whyNot.1: Repeating the message increases volume but still gives no evidence of understanding.
whyNot.2: Extra detail may even add to confusion; it does not check understanding.
whyNot.3: Copying in the sponsor widens distribution, not understanding.

explain.body: Anything that distorts the message between sender and receiver is a barrier, often called noise. The main ones: jargon, language, culture, distance, emotion, technology and information overload. The project manager's job is to anticipate them and choose words, timing and medium to get around them.

test.q: In the communication model, what is the term for anything that distorts a message between sender and receiver?
test.why: Noise (barriers) is anything that distorts or blocks the message on its way to being understood.

whyNot.0: The medium is the channel that carries the message, such as email or a meeting.
whyNot.1: Feedback is the receiver's response that confirms understanding.
whyNot.2: Encoding is the sender turning an idea into a message.
